note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Understand how learning works in a discipline's discourse community

evidence.title: Map of your discipline as a community of practice
evidence.example: You map your discipline as a community using Lave and Wenger's (1991) idea of legitimate peripheral participation: newcomers learn by taking part in real but limited ways and move towards full participation. You mark where you are now as a newcomer and the activities, such as seminars, reading and writing, that move you inward. This shows you understand how learning works in your discipline's discourse community (for example, a first-year archaeology student placing themselves relative to lecturers who excavate and publish).
evidence.artefact: A labelled diagram of your discipline's community showing your position and the activities that move you towards fuller participation.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

evidence.title: Notes from a research seminar on how the discipline argues
evidence.example: You attend a real event in your discipline's community, such as a departmental research seminar, a guest lecture or a learned society meeting, and note how people talk, argue and use evidence there. You then write a short account of what this taught you about how the discipline learns. This shows you understanding a discourse community from the inside (for example, a physics student noting how a speaker's results were questioned at a colloquium).
evidence.artefact: Event notes and a short account of the community's ways of talking, arguing and using evidence.
grounding: professional: Learns how a profession or organisation works, its norms, people and ways of knowing, on joining it.

capabilities.statement: Tell formative from summative assessment and engage with varied forms

evidence.title: Module assessments sorted and aligned to outcomes
evidence.example: You list the assessments in one module, label each formative or summative, and use Biggs' (1996) constructive alignment to show which learning outcome each is designed to check. You then note how you will use the formative tasks to prepare for the summative ones. This shows you can tell the two apart and engage with varied forms (for example, a first-year marketing student seeing that a practice pitch prepares for the assessed group presentation).
evidence.artefact: A module assessment table labelled formative or summative, each linked to an outcome, with your plan for using the formative tasks.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996

evidence.title: Optional formative draft used to improve a marked piece
evidence.example: You take part in a formative task you could skip, such as a draft submission, a practice quiz or a peer review, and use the feedback to change the final piece before it is marked. This shows you engaging with varied assessment forms and treating rehearsal as a chance to improve (for example, a film studies student submitting an essay plan for comment and restructuring the argument as a result).
evidence.artefact: Your formative draft with its feedback, beside the summative submission showing the changes you made.
grounding: professional: Uses practice runs, drafts and reviews as chances to improve before work is judged.

capabilities.statement: Tell active, constructivist learning from passive reception

evidence.title: Two study sessions compared as deep and surface approaches
evidence.example: You record two study sessions on the same reading, one spent rereading and highlighting and one spent questioning, summarising in your own words and linking to earlier topics. Using Marton and Saljo's (1976) distinction between deep and surface approaches, you explain which session was active and constructivist and what you could explain afterwards. This shows you can tell active learning from passive reception (for example, a philosophy student comparing their grasp of a Kant extract after each session).
evidence.artefact: Notes from both sessions side by side, with a short commentary classifying each approach and what you could explain afterwards.
grounding: ing:doc:approaches-to-learning-marton-saljo-1976

evidence.title: Learning a work task actively instead of waiting to be shown
evidence.example: In a job, volunteering or society role, you notice a point where you were waiting to be told what to do and instead learn it actively: asking questions, trying it and checking your understanding. You write up the contrast. This shows you distinguishing active from passive learning in practice (for example, a computing student in a summer IT support job learning a ticketing system by working through real requests rather than reading the manual).
evidence.artefact: A short before-and-after account of learning a task at work, confirmed by a note from your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Takes an active part in own learning at work rather than waiting to be trained.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

capabilities.statement: Interpret learning outcomes and how activities align to them

evidence.title: Alignment grid tracing outcomes to activities and assessment
evidence.example: You take the intended learning outcomes for a module, pick out the verb in each, and trace how lectures, seminars and the assessment are aligned to them, using Biggs' (1996) constructive alignment. Where an outcome has no clear matching activity, you note how you will practise it yourself. This shows you interpreting outcomes and how activities align to them (for example, a civil engineering student linking 'design a beam' to tutorial calculations and the design project).
evidence.artefact: An alignment grid: each outcome, its verb, the matching activities and assessment, and your own actions for any gaps.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996

evidence.title: Everyday tasks mapped to role objectives with a supervisor
evidence.example: In a job, placement or society role, you take the objectives or performance standards you are given, work out how your everyday tasks contribute to each, and discuss the mapping with your supervisor. This shows you reading objectives and seeing how tasks relate to them, as you do with learning outcomes (for example, a hospitality management student mapping hotel reception duties to the guest satisfaction targets in their appraisal).
evidence.artefact: A mapping of your tasks to your role objectives, annotated after discussion with your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Reads objectives and performance standards and sees how tasks and appraisal relate to them.

capabilities.statement: Turn feedback into an action plan through reflection

evidence.title: Feedback turned into an action plan by reflection-on-action
evidence.example: You take feedback on a marked assignment and use Schon's (1983) reflection-on-action to look back at the decisions you made while writing it, asking why you made them and what the feedback suggests instead. You turn this into an action plan with specific, dated changes for the next assignment. This shows you using reflective practice to turn feedback into improvement (for example, a social work student reviewing comments on how they applied legislation in a case study).
evidence.artefact: Annotated feedback, a reflection on your decisions and an action plan of specific, dated changes.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-practitioner-schon-1983

evidence.title: Supervisor feedback acted on through a short development plan
evidence.example: You turn appraisal or supervisor feedback from a job, placement or volunteering role into a short development plan, act on it over several weeks and review the outcome with the person who gave the feedback. This shows you using feedback to plan improvement beyond the classroom (for example, a retail management student acting on a shift manager's comments about handling customer complaints).
evidence.artefact: Feedback notes, your development plan and a follow-up review signed or emailed by your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Acts on appraisal and colleague feedback through a development plan.
professional: Vitae RDF B3: professional and career development

capabilities.statement: Apply self-regulated learning cycles to independent study

evidence.title: Two documented cycles of self-regulated independent study
evidence.example: You plan, monitor and review a block of independent study using Zimmerman's (2002) cyclical model of self-regulated learning: forethought (setting goals and strategies), performance (monitoring as you work) and self-reflection (evaluating results). You complete at least two full cycles and show how the second changed in light of the first. This shows you applying self-regulated learning to independent study (for example, a modern languages student preparing for an oral exam through weekly practice cycles).
evidence.artefact: Two completed cycle records, covering forethought, performance and self-reflection, showing what changed between the first and second.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)

evidence.title: Progress log kept across a live client brief
evidence.example: During a long independent project, such as a dissertation, a self-directed lab project or a live client brief, you set weekly goals, keep a progress log and adjust your approach at set review points, sharing the log with your supervisor. This shows you applying self-regulated cycles to real independent work (for example, a product design student running a twelve-week brief for a local charity).
evidence.artefact: A project progress log with weekly goals, monitoring notes and recorded adjustments, shared with your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Plans own work and development, monitors progress against goals and adjusts approach.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

capabilities.statement: Adapt to the demands of different types of assessment

evidence.title: Three assessment types compared by the thinking they demand
evidence.example: Across three assessment types, such as an exam, a reflective portfolio and a group report, you analyse the command verbs and criteria with Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001) to identify the level of thinking each demands, and adapt your preparation and writing to match. This shows you adapting to the demands of different types of assessment (for example, a politics student seeing that a policy brief asks them to evaluate and recommend, while an exam answer asks them to explain).
evidence.artefact: A comparison sheet for three assessments: verbs, Bloom's levels, and how you adapted your approach for each.
grounding: model: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001)

evidence.title: Briefing written for a real external audience
evidence.example: You produce work for a real audience in a form judged outside the university, such as a pitch to a business, a report for a community group or a funding bid for a society, and adapt your approach to that form's expectations. You note what differed from academic genres. This shows you adapting to the forms in which work is judged (for example, an environmental science student writing a two-page flood-risk briefing for a parish council).
evidence.artefact: The finished piece for the external audience, their response, and a short note on how you adapted to the form.
grounding: professional: Adapts to the forms in which work is judged: reports, pitches, reviews and audits.

capabilities.statement: Assess own and peers' work against marking criteria

evidence.title: Exemplar and own draft marked using Sadler's conditions
evidence.example: You mark an exemplar and then your own draft against the published marking criteria, using Sadler's (1989) conditions for improvement: knowing the standard, comparing your work with it and acting to close the gap. You justify each judgement with evidence from the text and compare your marks with a tutor's. This shows you assessing work against criteria (for example, a biomedical science student marking a lab report exemplar before self-assessing their own report).
evidence.artefact: A marked exemplar and self-assessed draft with criterion-by-criterion justifications, plus a comparison with the tutor's mark.
grounding: model: Conditions for closing the gap through feedback (Sadler 1989)

evidence.title: Criterion-based peer review in a team code review
evidence.example: You act as a reviewer in a real process, such as structured peer review on your module, editing for a society publication or a team code review, giving criterion-based comments on others' work before submission and receiving them on your own. This shows you reviewing work against agreed standards, as colleagues do before work is released (for example, a software engineering student reviewing teammates' pull requests against the team's coding standards).
evidence.artefact: Your written review comments mapped to the criteria, and the responses or changes they led to.
grounding: professional: Reviews own and colleagues' work against agreed standards before it is submitted or published.
professional: Carless and Boud (2018): making judgements

capabilities.statement: Use feedback in dialogue with tutors to sustain development across a degree

evidence.title: Cross-module feedback analysis using four features of feedback literacy
evidence.example: You review the feedback you have received across your degree and analyse it with Carless and Boud's (2018) four features of feedback literacy: appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect and taking action. You identify recurring themes, show how you acted on them, and set out how you will keep using feedback beyond the course. This shows you using feedback diagnostically to sustain development (for example, a master's student in education tracing a recurring comment about critical synthesis).
evidence.artefact: A cross-module feedback analysis with recurring themes, evidence of action taken and a plan linked to the four features.
grounding: ing:doc:feedback-literacy-carless-boud-2018

evidence.title: Feedback meetings you prepare for and lead across a term
evidence.example: You arrange and lead feedback conversations with a tutor, supervisor or manager over a term, bringing your own questions and a summary of what you have changed since the last meeting, and you record what you agree. This shows you seeking feedback actively and using dialogue to build on it over time (for example, a postgraduate translation student meeting a dissertation supervisor fortnightly with a list of queries on drafts).
evidence.artefact: Meeting records across a term showing your questions, the actions agreed and the changes made between meetings.
grounding: professional: Seeks feedback actively, discusses it with managers and colleagues and builds on it over time.
professional: Carless and Boud (2018): appreciating feedback, taking action
